The recent advancements in beam-based alignment techniques at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have achieved precise measurements of beam-beam closed orbit deviations, amounting to approximately half a millimeter throughout the entire machine. To make use of this detailed information and further improve beam-based alignment in future machines like the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), various interpretation models have been developed and reviewed. These models incorporate existing closed orbit data to derive more explicit and locally valid measurements of beam-beam interactions. Notable techniques such as filling new skew quadrupole channels with parameters of 1 mm and 1 mrad have been successfully applied to the LHC and will also be utilized in the HL-LHC. However, utilizing multipole errors from thin beam-based alignment magnets has demonstrated limited effectiveness due to issues with decoupling in the horizontal and vertical planes. As an alternative approach, this study explores the potential of using octupole magnets to determine the relative alignment of beams by evaluating its sensitivity to beam-based alignment parameters without compromising the HL-LHC commissioning schedule.

This research develops a robust optimal distributed controller for multi-agent systems with malicious members in varying networks. We develop a novel cooperative communication protocol that guarantees optimized system performance, despite dynamic topologies and malicious agents, by ensuring the security of communication among non-malicious agents, a controller, and adaptive graph topologies. A novel adaptive control law is proposed to ensure the feasibility of a communication protocol across all agents, resulting in an optimal solution to the quadratic performance index. The controller's decision-making process is explained through the Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) framework. The proposed method's effectiveness and robustness are validated through numerical simulations.

The upcoming generation of large-scale surveys like Euclid, DESIS, and LSST will produce high-precision data on the cosmic structure, specifically on the distribution of galaxies and clusters. Achieving this level of accuracy requires accounting for instrumental systematic effects, such as photometric zero-point variations caused by thermal fluctuations in the spectrograph, which can cause errors in measuring the cosmic structure on large scales. Using synthetic data that mimics the effects of these systematics, researchers can develop and test correction methods on a realistic basis. This study explores the potential impact of these systematics on our understanding of the universe's structure by analyzing their effect on the cosmic spectrum of density fluctuations. A simple method is created to generate realistic data that includes the effect of thermal drift, which is then used to create a model of how the universe's structure is distributed on a large scale. Additionally, this study creates methods to identify and correct these systematics, such as by incorporating their pattern into our current models of the universe's structure. Furthermore, it demonstrates how future surveys can accurately measure the universe's structure, such as baryon acoustic oscillations, even in the presence of these systematics, with high levels of precision.

The BART model demonstrated exceptional accuracy in predicting partial tree structures, which are more complex than the binary trees it was able to order correctly. To investigate this limitation, we created a new task called Partial Tree Linearization (PTL) and found that BART's performance improved significantly when we provided a linearized version of the partial tree instead of just the set of parent-child relationships. This suggests that natural language syntax is inherently more similar to partial tree structures that have non-binary branching patterns, particularly those with bigram and bigram-like connections.

Our study focuses on developing detection methods for deepfakes that are effective across different devices and applications. To achieve this goal, we introduce three innovative loss functions designed to strengthen the consistency and reliability of deepfake classification networks. Our first approach, Consistency Cross-Stroke Loss, aims to minimize discrepancies in pixel-level reconstructions by leveraging real data from multiple domains. Our second and third methods, Domain-Agnostic Attention Loss and Multi-Domain Attention Loss, leverage attention mechanisms to identify and incorporate valuable information from various domains. Our experimental results demonstrate that our proposed methods significantly enhance the performance of deepfake detection networks, particularly when dealing with unfamiliar data.

Recently, M. S. Ashbaugh and T. H. Yang introduced a method to evaluate the maximum angle between any pair of directions in a high-dimensional conformably embedded sphere. They proved that if this angle is less than 135 degrees in a specific way, the embedding must be linear. However, this condition needs to be evaluated for more complex scenarios where the maximum angle is achieved by a larger set of directions. To address this, we define the angle function in a way that generalizes the previously defined version and is capable of handling cases where multiple directions form the deciding factor. Then, we examine the properties of the angle function in two types of spaces: the spectral maximum angle and the geodesic maximum angle. We discover that the generalised version of the maximum angle function is capable of characterizing linear conformal maps.

We establish inequalities involving isomorphism classes of orders within specific number fields with an identical residue field size $q$. These inequalities, formed by taking powers of isomorphism classes, allow us to determine when number fields share the same isomorphism types as their orders. Notably, our research extends previous work by Jacobson and Taylor-James by generalizing it to broader classes of non-maximal orders. Our findings are illustrated through the use of Minkowski's dimension.

We demonstrate that the basis $\bar{\bf f}\theta$ of the quantum group ${\bf U}_q(\frak{g})$ maintains invariance under the Lusztid braid group action and possesses well-defined transformations under the Dynkin automorphisms. These properties enable us to construct the ${\bf U}_q(\frak{g})$-module basis $\bar{\bf V}$ associated with the fundamental matrix ${\bf T}$ of the L-operator, which is shown to possess the positive structure. Furthermore, this construction can be extended to the quantum affine algebra ${\bf U}_q(\widehat{\frak{g}}))$. We provide explicit examples of this construction for the affine algebras of type A and C. These findings are further explored in collaboration with A. Ramy and A. Sorey.

The Forsage blockchain game, which is integral to the pyramidal scheme, saw a significant majority of its participants, approximately 94%, suffer financial losses before the scheme's collapse on the 30th of September 2020. The paper delves into the intricate rules of Forsage, conducts simulations to model the scheme's dynamics, and presents the data from blockchain records, providing insights into the scheme's accounting practices and user experiences. Furthermore, it presents mathematical findings on the expected returns of Forsage, categorizing them based on the hierarchy of contributors.

The Milky Way's globular cluster population numbers in the low-to-medium heliocentric distance range of 3 to 10 kiloparsecs, which is crucial for understanding their overall distribution. However, determining the ages and distances of less well-studied clusters presents a challenge. We utilized Gaia DR2 data to construct initial color-magnitude diagrams for five potential clusters, each containing over a thousand red giant branch stars, located within 5 to 10 kiloparsecs. Based on these diagrams, we determined that these clusters have ages spanning 1 to 10 billion years, making them invaluable for comprehending both the spherical component's star formation history and the contrast between ancient and more recent populations. The combined ages and locations of these clusters can contribute to refining the Milky Way's globular cluster model.

We define and analyze tensor networks as computational frameworks for a specific type of quantum error-correcting stabilizer states, where each component of the network functions as a unitary gate acting on several qubits. Our research also develops methods to convert between different tensor network representations of the same code, even when the network comprises only one type of tensor serving as a minimal description. We further examine the relationship between these tensor networks and the Toffoli gate, demonstrating that a large set of non-linear functions can be captured by expanding tensor networks that include the Toffoli gate. Our discussion includes an in-depth examination of the computational complexity of simulating tensor networks with a single-tensor types, revealing that this task is exponentially challenging, specifically belonging to the class of problems known as #P-complete.

Stripe process missing data modeling has been used to handle incomplete data
for structured time series, and recent advancements have applied it to various
fields with several innovations in data imputation methods.  However, these
models assume processes without interruptions and have been applied to diverse
business scenarios such as customer orders and shipments.  In contrast, high
variance in early process stages and extensive incomplete data in later stages
are common issues in many business processes, and these issues have been shown
to be effectively addressed with current research methods.  Despite these
findings, high variance and incomplete data aspects have not been explored in
specific locations, and consequently our work uses real-world data from an
online retail company to capture various interruptions and incomplete data from
five locations, and regression models are employed to analyze patterns of high
variance and incomplete data.  Notably, we discover that models' performance
degrades substantially across different process stages and regions, and thus
concepts to address high residual variance and missing data are introduced in
our contribution to improve stripe process imputation under interruptions and
incomplete data with high variance.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that our
contribution significantly enhances the accuracy of retailed data by as much as
10% and reduces average residual variance by as much as 16%.  Finally, videos
of available data patterns and retailed data reconstruction are provided to
validate the effectiveness of our approach.

This research investigates the connection between the behavior of functions and their Fourier transforms within a specific class of spaces characterized by distinct growth rates in different domains. We establish inequalities describing the maximum size of functions, based on the size of their Fourier transforms and vice versa. These inequalities are consistent with previously established results and provide a more general, uniform approach to understanding these relationships.

Researchers studied a star known as AD Leo with the help of the Spitzer Space Telescope, specifically using its infrared detectors during a significant flare that was observed in visible light. They found that the size of the electron clouds in the star varied during the flare, with their typical density ranging from 0.1 to 1 times 10^11 times per square centimeter. They also discovered that the movement of these electron clouds was influenced by the extent of a particular type of radiation emitted by the star. Additionally, they estimated that the flames caused by the flare contained temperatures of up to a few times 10^4 Kelvin, with sizes ranging from 10^9 to 10^10 centimeters. Based on these findings, the authors believe that the movement of electron clouds can be used to predict the future behavior of the stars, which in turn can affect the safety of satellites and astronauts in space.

Neural network models gaining widespread use are vulnerable to label-misclassification through data manipulation techniques such as adding noise, adjusting aspect ratios, and color space swaps. Point cloud models can also be subjected to such robustness attacks. Inspired by certification frameworks established in the scalar and image domains, we propose a novel certifiability standard against a "twisting" transformation that simultaneously deforms space by rotating and translating the origin, pointwise adding noise, and masking random elements. Point cloud models can be subjected to this complex transformation. Our TPC (Certifiability against Point Cloud Twisting) framework enables training without compromising performance, as it utilizes an auxiliary loss function and a novel generative discriminator that distinguishes between original and manipulated, masked data. Our experimental results in both simple and complex scenarios demonstrate a substantial improvement in models' guarantees against the twisting transformation while maintaining high accuracy rates.

Researchers examined the energy consumption of the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance during its creation, focusing on its closure in the energy domain for both ground and excited states and tracking how energy is lost to various states through various emission channels. Utilizing the Random Phase Approximation, they studied a 16-electron system and attributed certain inelastic scattering outcomes to transitions between specific state combinations, explaining the formation of its energy state consumption distribution. Their findings showed that elastic scattering dominates above a certain energy range, while significant energy is consumed through gamma emission at lower energies, with the RPA framework effectively capturing its overall behavior.

Nonlinear dynamical systems often exhibit complex behaviors that are difficult to model and understand.  The Koopman operator framework provides a powerful alternative approach by capturing the nonlinear dynamics through a linear representation in a suitable infinite-dimensional space, enabling the use of linear tools for analysis.  Recently, data-driven methods have been developed to construct approximations of the Koopman operator directly from observed trajectories, without requiring explicit knowledge of the underlying system equations.  However, these approaches typically rely on the availability of state trajectories throughout the phase space.  In this paper, we address the challenge of learning the Koopman operator when only time-series data in the form of observations at discrete points is available.  We introduce a novel closure method based on orthogonal polynomials that can construct data-driven bases and derive the linear evolution operator purely from observed data, bypassing the need for state trajectories.  Numerical experiments on various test cases, including the Kolmogorov equation, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

To address the issue of neural text generation producing sentences with excessive redundancy, we propose a novel SparseGAN framework that leverages a sparse attention mechanism. By limiting the number of recurrent updates and attention heads in specific stages, our approach forces diversity into generated sentences while maintaining their coherence. We evaluate the method on character- and word-level generation tasks using the Wikipedia dump and WMT'14 datasets, demonstrating that sparse sampling can effectively diversify generated text without compromising its quality. Our research also reveals that rare tokens require more time steps to emerge and that standard attention diversity decreases as text rarity increases.

The concept of interstellar panspermia suggests that complex life could be spread between galaxies, but this theory neglects the harsh conditions found in many stellar environments. To overcome this limitation, a new framework is introduced that assesses suitable conditions for interstellar panspermia by examining the relationship between stellar mass and various environmental factors. This framework categorizes suitable conditions for complex life on a condition-suitability index from 3 to 1, indicating that certain conditions could allow seeds of life to survive and grow, while others might only let them endure temporarily. Detailed examinations of various stellar environments reveal that some conditions are more favorable for interstellar panspermia, including open clusters and associations around low-mass stars, while others are less suitable, such as stellar disks of Wolf-Rayet stars. This framework provides valuable guidance for evaluating the potential for life to spread between galaxies and could influence the strategy for searching for life on other planets.

Researchers utilized spatial capture-recurrence methodology applied to camera traps, which recorded captures and displacements of individual animals based on their photo locations. Data from these records came from over 200 camera traps situated in the Calanca Valley, Italy, resulting in data from 19 individual red deer and 444 camera traps operating for one year. Researchers employed an 8th order polynomial utility model to characterize the relationship between camera trap location and trapping probability, which was validated against simpler models such as logistic regression and thin-plate smoothing. Results showed that the polynomial model provided the most accurate fit and allowed estimation of density across various spatial areas. Furthermore, this study's density estimates were validated against previous SCR model estimates from the same area and additional field data.

The impact dynamics across multiple network layers are modeled using a simplified framework, where nodes connect to one another based on probabilistic rules and respond with varying intensities to external stimuli. This approach is applicable to various scenarios, including communication between networks, synchronization of coupled systems, and wave propagation. Our analysis focuses on assessing the stability of states within multilayer networks, revealing that the network's structure can significantly influence the connectedness across layers, as well as the evolution of connections and intensities over time. Our theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations, exploring the effects of the probability of interlayer connections, the likelihood of node-to-node connections, and the tendency for nodes to increase their connection intensity.

Given two differential modules over the ring of analytic functions, we define the relationship where the first is considered parametrized by the second if its solution space is completely contained within that of the second. This paper investigates the properties of this "parametrized by" relation and provides a method to determine when an operator is parametrized by another. It also explores the set of all operators that would require the first operator, demonstrating it has both being closed and being quasi-hereditary. Furthermore, we establish that the "parametrized by" relation is behaved well with regard to restriction and composition operations.

The advent of sophisticated text-based programming languages and tools has significantly benefited programmers, despite these advantages, errors in code can lead to costly and time-consuming issues if not rectified. To mitigate this, we've developed a comprehensive code testing environment that includes a automated system for locating and correcting mistakes. This, in turn, leverages the full potential of efficient algorithms. The text-based interface of the environment allows programmers to utilize our specialized data structures and algorithms, which are optimized for handling large datasets. We highlight several examples, including a reverse linked list algorithm and a web crawler that can process millions of pages within minutes. Additionally, we highlight essential techniques for speed enhancement, including sorting, hash tables, and memory allocation strategies.

In the study of root systems, particularly those of types A_l and D_l, there is a distinctive, uniquely identifiable root known as the maximal root, which has distinctive properties that set it apart from other roots. This distinctive root plays a significant role in mathematical structures such as Lie algebras and geometric configurations like flag varieties and torus orbits. A maximal root is distinguished by having the largest possible length and can be identified by having the highest coefficient in the fundamental weight with the smallest index. This root has the largest possible length, coefficient with the fundamental weight of the smallest index and is absent in the set of short roots. In the context of Lie algebras, the maximal root plays a significant role in determining the set of theta roots, which in turn plays a role in defining subsets of the set of all roots that have desirable combinatorial properties. In this study, we provide a way to determine the maximal root based on the set of simple roots, the lengths of the set of all roots, and the set of short roots in types A_l and D_l.

This work presents a novel solution to the challenge of estimating a large-scale network's size in a distributed setting. We have developed a rapidly executing algorithm capable of estimating the size of a notewwork without the need for a central authority, where each node can assign random identifiers and establish incoming links based on these randomly assigned IDs. Our proposed algorithm is suitable for networks where nodes have limited capabilities and can only establish a minimal number of incoming links. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by utilizing the Elastic Chasms model to evaluate packet loss rates, with results showing that the algorithm can estimate a 10 Tera-scale network with remarkable accuracy, even in networks producing up to 1 Gbps of traffic across 1 million nodes, without the need for centralized management.

To address the limitations of parametric methods in estimating the size of queuing systems, a novel, straightforward approach was developed that utilizes the probability distribution of the queuing length. With the aid of the Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm, the proposed method demonstrates superior accuracy in evaluating queue length compared to parametric techniques, especially when dealing with outliers. Additionally, it provides a more precise assessment of service times' tail distributions than traditional parametric approaches.

This definition, which includes a reinterpreted six-dimensional delta function, leads to a distinct formulation of the Hamiltonian constraint.配合 this, we employ the "standard" method for handling conformal factors using the $h$-hypothesis. This approach allows us to solve the Hamiltonian constraint using six-dimensional methods, effectively decoupling it from the Hamiltonian constraint. We demonstrate this decoupling and solution for both regular grids and those containing delta functions. Finally, we introduce a discrete version of our approach, which incorporates a new handling of conformal factors using the $h$-hypothesis, thus decoupling their treatment from the rest of the constraints.

Antiferromagnetic anomalous Nernst effect (AFANE) has never been observed in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites until now, where it is prominently displayed by the $Ru_2RuSi_3$ compound. The $Ru_2RuSi_3$ material exhibits strong ANE and TH effects as a direct consequence of its antiferromagnetic properties. The $Ru$ sublattices in $Ru_2RuSi_3$ are either ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic, while the $Si$ sublattice is also ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic, and these different magnetic configurations contribute to the ANE and AFNE effects. The ANE is primarily driven by the $Ru$ sublattice, and its temperature dependence is similar to that of magnetic susceptibility. Furthermore, $Ru_2RuSi_3$ displays the Seebeck effect with a high value of 14.5 $\mu$V/K, and its ANE performance is superior to that of $Ru_2CoSi_3$ and $Ru_2RhSi_3$. The exceptional ANE and AFNE properties of $Ru_2RuSi_3$ make it a prime candidate for enhancing ANE and TH device performance.

We define non-autonomous obstacle problems and examine the impact of an obstacle's gradient sobolev regularity. These cocycles are found to be directly related to the study of crystalline modules, and an indirect connection is also established between them and the representation of groups, specifically the Galois group, in a linear manner. Building on prior research by Breuer, we construct a representation that has an null component and utilizes the linear representation from the work of Carlet and Shu as well as a specific type of distribution, called K-stationary, to describe this cocycle. Furthermore, we prove that the set of G_K-Artin-Sheier cocycles is an abelian group, and demonstrate that the aforementioned representation restricts to the type of linear representation that preserves certain properties under reduction, and may potentially include the class of crystalline types, and additionally, we show an indirect relationship with the set of linear representations that have a monotone behavior, and can perhaps encompass the type known as rational monodromy, and we further examine the connection between the linear representation from the work of Shu and the linear representation from the work of Tsuzuku.

A conic measure-scale-flatness meso concept has been introduced for hypersurfaces within a given mean curvature limit, situated in a spacetime environment.  This intermediate concept serves a purpose analogous to compactness, enabling the extraction of compact subsets from sets with message-scale-flat properties under section slicing and closure operations.  Additionally, the message flatness property exhibits stability under the $C^1$-message, allowing for the discernment of finite meso-topologies from the sliced surfaces of surfaces with message-scale-flatness, endowed with conic conic cones.

To enhance damage detection in easily damaged composites, a novel approach has been developed, tailored for materials that undergo significant structural changes, by integrating a genetic algorithm, specifically the NSGA-II, into the backpropagation algorithm for more accurate and efficient neural network optimization. This method's effectiveness was extensively tested on a difficult detection case involving a damaged simple beam, demonstrating its ability to accurately locate various types of damage and identify multiple damages simultaneously, while also minimizing the energy consumed during training by producing multiple optimal solutions with different energy consumptions. The results, obtained using multiple performance indicators, showcase the method's superior accuracy and efficiency in comparing it to the conventional single-optimal solutions.

We investigate the dynamics of a predator-prey relationship governed by the Lotka-Volterra model, where the decisions of species to cooperate, act neutrally, or compete are driven by varying levels of intelligence. We explore how the combined effects of a predator's and prey's intelligence, characterized by their problem-solving strategies, influence the stability of the system and its resilience to random disturbances. Notably, we find that when both species exhibit cooperative tendencies, the system is more prone to sudden collapses, in contrast to the robust fluctuations observed when both species adopt neutral competition strategies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system's behavior can be categorized into distinct phases, including an intelligent co-existence phase, where the population reaches a stable state determined by the levels of problem-solved by the predator and prey. Our study also reveals that the predator-prey dynamics can be harnessed to engineer mechanisms for size-standardization with enhanced precision.

An approach based on basic geometric vector principles is applied to establish vector integral identities, utilizing Green's first identity for vectors. These methods provide alternative proofs for conventional results and establish new relations through their approach.

The recent measurement of the muon g-2 anomaly has significant implications for the nature of dark matter, particularly when combined with constraints from direct detection and indirect observation methods. To explore this intersection, theoretical models have been examined, including those involving the scalar singlet, the scalar di-doublet, and the complex scalar field within the "Majoron" or "2HDM + scalar lepton number violating" frameworks, when specific terms such as $\bar{e}_1 \phi_1 s$, $\bar{e}_2 \phi_2 s$, and $\bar{\tau}_1 \phi_1 s + \bar{\tau}_2 \phi_2 i s$ are considered. To further understand the relationship between the $(g-2)_\mu$ and dark matter when their interaction occurs through this scalar field, we explored an intermediate framework, referred to as "HDM$+e_\tau$" scenario, where the scalar field also gives mass to the heaviest neutral Higgs boson and the muon. However, this model is quickly ruled out due to large contributions from loop processes, prompting us to propose utilizing the muon electric and magnetic capture modes in the next generation of the muon $g-2$ experiment. Additionally, we found that a broader parameter space can be explored through direct detection, microlens, and loop processes, while constraints from neutral meson decay and radiative process remain rather limited.

The spin-three Ward identities, which we recently derived, provide a comprehensive framework for exploring and extending the concept of higher-spin symmetry beyond its original scope in Toda conformal field theories. By applying this framework to various aspects, such as the Liouville TBA, the Tdual TBA, and the free energy of AdS/CFT, we can systematically expand our understanding of the theory in the large-c limit. Through this process, we will explore a higher-genus Toda conformal field theory, which can be viewed as a dual to Liouville TBA at a higher genus, and will also explore the free energy of AdS$_3$ / Simplicial Matter CFT beyond its initial expansion, gaining a deeper understanding of the theory's properties and behaviors.

We demonstrate that the class of biautomatic groups includes uniform lattices within the isometry group of a finite-rank, discrete valuation field's type field. This achievement further indicates that isometry groups of valuation fields of a certain category are both computably presentable and subgroup presentable.

Recent advancements in assistive and restorative technologies for individuals with mobility limitations promise to predict the intention to walk and seamlessly provide assistance.  However, existing methodologies primarily focus on executing pre-programmed walking patterns in response to external triggers and fail to account for nuanced decisions humans make while navigating different terrains and obstacles.  To address this limitation, there is a pressing need for cutting-edge prosthetic and assistive devices that can interpret signals indicating various foot placements on sole sensors and execute corresponding walking patterns seamlessly.  In this study, we present a novel deep learning-based framework utilizing a convolutional recurrent network to interpret electrocorticographic (ECoG) brain signals and execute various foot placement patterns during overground walking.  In this study, we employed data from four subjects during overground walking and compared the accuracy of our model in predicting foot placement when using only unilateral vs. bilateral foot placement ECoG signals.  In this study, we achieved remarkable accuracy rates of 95.5% using unilateral and 97.3% using bilateral foot placement ECoG signals, which is significantly more accurate than traditional deep learning networks.  In this study, we demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed CNN-CR network and the feasibility of encoding various foot placement patterns during overground walking, which is a crucial step towards developing a predictive brain-machine interface for seamless integration between the human brain and machine during overground walking.

When a right-angled Artin group acts on a tree with a specific vertex being fixed, the set of edges connecting the fixed vertex to its own connected component can be shown to have a finite index. This paper proves these settings are topologically unique, extending a previous finding by M. L. Souto for free groups.

Dynamic temporal networks exhibiting seasonal patterns and abrupt changes pose significant challenges to prediction models. Existing static or time-sequential models fail to capture both periodic fluctuations and sudden events simultaneously. We propose DECENNT, a novel variational autoencoder-based framework for efficient and robust representation of dynamic graphs. DECENNT comprises two components: a periodic component modeled using an unrolled graph autoencoder and a sparse component modeled with a graph attention network. By decomposing the graph structure into these two aspects, DECENNT achieves a dual benefit: it efficiently represents the graph by avoiding node-level adjacency matrix operations and precisely predicts sudden events through the graph attention network. We evaluate DECENNT on real-world datasets and it outperforms 9 state-of-the-art methods in a comprehensive benchmark, demonstrating its superior performance in handling the complexity of dynamic graph representation. Additionally, DECENNT exhibits enhanced computational efficiency, predicting the $t$-th time step $N$ steps ahead with a time complexity of ${\mathcal{O}}(N{\text{time}}_1 +{\mathcal{O}}_2)$, where ${\text{time}}_1$ is the representation period and ${\mathcal{O}}_2$ is the graph attention network's representation cost at the target node. Our DECENNT project is hosted at this link: https://github.com/DECENNT/DECENNT.

A critical aspect of object detection involves differentiating between biological and non-biological objects, a distinction that is primarily based on the movement patterns of the objects. However, the ambiguity of object motion can pose challenges in developing reliable automatic detection systems. To address this challenge, a novel classification framework has been proposed that differentiates between objects based on the assumption that the movement of biological objects adheres to the 'Biological Motion Regularity' pattern, whereas the movement of non-biological objects is subject to the 'Non-Biological Motion Regularity' pattern. A convolutional neural network-based method has been developed to extract motion features from the input image sequence, which are further refined using the K-S test to distinguish between the two types of object motion. The proposed framework demonstrates a biological vs. non-biological classification accuracy of 90% in the WOMBAs dataset, a significant improvement over existing methods.

The algorithm leverons inception depth, which enables a comparison to the original Neumann algorithm applied multiple times, yielding a higher infinity norm bound on the effective resistance. A key finding is that a greater inception depth results in a higher Neumann algorithm application depth required to achieve a specific accuracy, notably a depth of $O(d^2/\delta \ln(1/\delta))$ for a relative error of $\delta$. Furthermore, incorporating the concept of inception depth permits more concise proof that the Nested Neumann algorithm converges and near-by Neumann algorithm applications can be significantly reduced to an infinity norm proximity measure with a dependence of Neumann algorithm application depth proportional to the number of nodes. Additionally, incorporating the inception depth notion permits an externalization of the algorithm and serves as the foundation for an approximate version of the Nested Neumann algorithm utilizing effective resistance sampling and depth reduction based on a sampling variant of multiplicative weights.

The application of topology in physics has seen growth across various fields, but understanding how to identify the topological properties of an Anderson insulator and dynamically controlling its topological character has been a challenge. By combining spin-orbit coupling with disorder in a two-dimensional nonreciprocal quantum lattice model, we overcame this difficulty. Through the calculation of the invariant known as the diagonal winding number, we were able to demonstrate that the identification and dynamic evolution of topological properties are feasible. A numerical approach based on the diagonal Green function enabled us to observe the evolution of the winding number in systems subject to disorder. In addition, we found that the diagonal density of states can serve as a diagnostic tool to detect the topological nature of an Anderson insulator and that a particular on-site potential can be used to manipulate its behavior. These discoveries highlight the potential of our model system as a practical platform for applying the distinctive features of Anderson topological phases.

We investigate the communication efficiency of algorithms in the setting of contextual linear bandits, where the problem's scale is defined by the understanding that agents should handle inputs and output data without being computationally hindered by the problem's size. Our approach involves developing two methods that achieve significant reductions in data transmission while maintaining an optimal regret minimization performance that is comparable to noncommunicating contextual linear bandits, contextual linear bandits with nonnegative parameters, and even simpler linear bandits. Our initial contribution addresses a wide range of problems, including those without contextual information and with various levels of data sparsity, demonstrating that even a minimal amount of communication can lead to an infinitely larger, infinite-dimensional problems to be solved effectively. Subsequently, we demonstrate that problems with contextual information and with a bounded norm can be handled such that their regression bases' dimensions are equal to that of the problem's input space plus one, thereby achieving a communicational reduction that is applicable to a wide variety of linear bandit problems, regardless of the dimensionality of their regression bases, which could be thousands of times larger than the dimension of the context. Our achievement relies on achieving an otherwise extremely high-dimensional problems to be solved effectively with data transmission that is equal to the dimension of the context plus one, thereby allowing a context with a dimension of a thousand times larger than the regression base's dimension to be handled such that the data transmission is equal to that plus one.

The transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons, specifically pions, K mesons, and protons, were analyzed in collisions producing 2%, 10%, 30%, 70%, and 100% central centrality. These distributions were examined across a wide range of transverse momenta from 0.2 to 8 GeV/c for various centralities and initial multiplicities. The data revealed that the slope parameters, $\T0$, of exponential fits to the p_T distributions of hadrons, primarily determined by the initial transport coefficient in a quasi-perfect fluid, increase with initial multiplicity and centrality. Notably, the $\T0$ values for protons and pions were nearly identical in the investigated p_T range, implying that radiative corrections, which become more prominent at higher initial momenta, do not significantly impact their average values. The results also showed that the initial transport coefficient, characterized by the $\T0$ parameter, continuously rises with initial multiplicity, described by a power law with an exponent of approximately 1.2, a finding that can be utilized to estimate the initial transport coefficient for heavy ion collisions.

This study employs a multiple-time-step integration method (MTSA) to simulate particles in a flow field, combining the MTSA with a symmetric time-discrete numerical method for accurate and efficient computation. By selectively applying smaller time-steps to particle movements while maintaining larger time-steps for flow solvers, our proposed approach significantly reduces computational costs without compromising numerical accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that our method can achieve the same level of numerical accuracy as traditional single-time-step simulations, but with significantly smaller time-steps. Moreover, we found that a two-time-step configuration delivers the same level of accuracy as a single-time-step simulation, but with substantially reduced computation costs, making it an ideal compromise between accuracy and efficiency for engineering applications.

The primary objective of this study lies in the exploration of the equation $7^n = a^3 + b^3$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers that are relatively prime to each other. The problem can be broken down into three cases based on the value of $n$, which can be 2,3, or any other integer greater than 3. In the first case, we utilize the work of Ljunggren to demonstrate that the only solution to the equation when $n = 2$ is $(a,b) = (1,2)$. The second case, where $n = 3$, is resolved using the properties of elliptic curves, yielding the solution $(a,b) = (8,4)$. Finally, in the third case, we use the method of descent in conjunction with modular forms to establish that there are no solutions to the equation.

This research develops and analyzes a simple robotic hopper with leg stiffness, aiming to enhance trajectory tracking on a compliant surface through feedback control. We derive equations for the robot's hopping dynamics, based on a mass-spring system, and develop a controlled hopping strategy with variable leg stiffness. Results from both discrete jumps and continuous ground contact demonstrate that feedback control, coupled with leg stiffness modulation, enables accurate tracking of desired trajectories. Furthermore, we identify conditions where hopping can become unstable and leg stiffness must be adjusted to maintain stability as ground compliance increases. Notably, beyond a certain level of ground compliance, no amount of stiffness can ensure stable hopping.

A researcher has derived an expression for the non-relativistic color charge radius of mesons, including hybrids, within the framework of the potential model. The calculation involves the use of the linear covariant gauge and the complete QCD potential, consisting of Coulombic, string, and spin-orbit components. The charge radii of light mesons have been computed and fall within an 8 MeV$^{2}$c$^{-2}$ range. Notably, the string contribution has a minimal impact, amounting to 3% for quark flavors, and a larger 12% for heavy charmonium and bottomonium states.

Quantum annealing is anticipated to efficiently solve a wide range of challenging optimization problems in the future.  However, its practical application remains limited due to a significant energy gap that anneals slowly near the highest state during the process.  We investigate the state gap during an increasingly complex simulation protocol, which includes a simulated thermalization phase, and employ higher-order expansions to analyze the resulting state gap dynamics.  Our investigation reveals that the state gap can significantly increase when thermalization is combined with a linear drive, and that this combination can result in a state gap that is two orders of magnitude larger than that of the standard protocol.  These findings are indicative of a expansion regime that can be expected to persist for a substantial period of time, and they are consistent with the principles of thermal quantum annealing.  Such results may provide a pathway to overcoming the current state gap bottleneck and could lead to optimized quantum annealing protocols that can solve more complex problems in less time.

We employ a method combining tight-binding modeling, COHSEX correction for exchange and correlation effects, and Berry-phase calculations to analyze the electronic properties of metallic nickelates, specifically 3d metal Ni in a filling state of two-thirds. Our study reveals the existence of flat, high-energy bands in nickelates that hinder the development of strong correlations and render many-body mechanisms, essential for characteristics like magnetism and superconductivity, unlikely. Consequently, we find that nickelates exhibit prominent intrashell d-d optical transitions but struggle to meet criteria for 5g orbital participation. Our insights are applicable to a broad spectrum of metallic compounds, encompassing transition metal chalcogenides, carbides, and nitrides.

This article investigates the properties of quark stars in an environment where the strong force behaves differently, specifically when a transition from confined to deconfined phases occurs abruptly. It examines the impact of this deconfinement transition on the structure of neutron stars by analyzing phase diagrams and studying various star configurations. A new theoretical model model is modelled to represent this transition, and the model is adjusted using data from laboratory experiments and heavy particle collisions. It is found that using this model allows for the description of heavy particle observations while also complying with observations of neutron collisions. Furthermore, it is discovered that the characteristics of quark stars, when observed, can distinguish between smooth transitions from confined to deconfinement phases and provide insights into the behavior of the phase during the transition.

Compass models are available in various materials, and their number variance is found to be favorable for estimating damping parameters and driving thresholds for phase clocks and memory devices. A classical compass state allows for accurate estimation of these parameters with a number variance that can be compared to other complex compass state variants. When the number variance is plotted against the mean number of $z$-component spins, it reveals that the z-basis compass state is optimal for estimating parameters and that its performance declines with increasing system size, prompting the exploration of non-standard $z$-bases to improve its metrological applications.

We investigated the cooling efficiency within the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, particularly in relation to the formation of ice on particles and their interaction with atmospheric processes. To better understand this phenomenon, we developed a model that incorporates thermal, solid-liquid phase transitions, DANA, and molecular vibrations for $H_2O$. By examining the effects of these factors, our study focused on how $H_2O$ influences cooling in different disk regions. Our model successfully replicated the properties of the "U-shaped" cooling curve observed in the outer disk. We found that in warm disk regions, where $H_2O$ is in a gaseous state, vibrational and rotational modes primarily contribute to emission and cooling. Conversely, in colder regions where ices form, our model replicates the surface temperature at which cooling becomes inefficient, matching the sublimation temperature of $H_2O$ in the gaseous and liquid phases. We observed that the latent heat of sublimation plays a crucial role in determining this surface temperature at the phase transition boundary. Additionally, we discovered that the heat capacity of ices also plays a significant role in the outer disk, as it can become trapped in a solid state even at temperatures above the sublimation point. This behavior was more impactful than the release of latent heat during the freezing process. Moreover, we found that the dust can remain in a cold state even at temperatures above the sublimation point in the warm inner disk region

This study focuses on harmonic functions satisfying a specific condition, $\\left|\\nabla u(p)\\right|^2\\leqslant λu(p)^2+μ$, within the framework of gradient shrinking Ricci solitons of dimension $n$. We establish a similar inequality for harmonic functions on the base manifold when considering a harmonic map from a spin$^{c}$ Dirac operator. Additionally, under a dimensionality constraint, $λ+\\frac{f}{2}+\\frac{μ+n}{4}>0$, we prove the existence of a polynomial relationship between the harmonic map and its target.

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have fueled public trust in the technology, prompting calls for increased transparency and safety standards. Unfortunately, this growing dependence makes deep learning models particularly susceptible to backdoor vulnerabilities, which can be triggered to misclassify specific inputs while maintaining high accuracy in normal operations. Although existing research has explored highly complex backdoor methods that adapt to unknown environments and cannot rely on clean training data, most studies lack the flexibility to execute dynamic attacks, where the model remains uninformed about targeted labels during training. This particular study develops two novel backdoor techniques that dynamic forms can take, one of which exploits training pauses in cloud environments, and the other exploits device storage limitations, respectively. These methods are explored across diverse classification tasks, including character, speech, and medical image classification, and demonstrate that subtle model alterations can lead to high-precision backdoor attacks without compromising model generalization. The code for this study is available on GitHub.

Recent Gaia Data Release 2 allows for the determination of solar system object parallax at high precision, particularly for objects with a low Earth orbital plane inclination. However, the apparent movement of these objects is influenced more by the precession, nutation, and proper motion of the Earth than by the object's orbital movement, posing a challenge in deriving precise distances to them. A significant discovery made with GDR2 astrometry shows a persistent relationship between an object's distance estimation error and its latitude relative to the Earth's orbit, indicating a systematic uncertainty in position measurements that varies with latitude. Utilizing the vector parallax and semi-major axis from GDR2, research on six active comets and three inactive ones yields an estimated ratio of orbital movement to Earth's motion of 0.73 with a standard of 0.05, enabling the extraction of a cometary place error of 0''.2, which accounts for the previously unexplained distance-related mistake.

Our research group is developing an open question answering system, which the project's primary focus is on integrating external knowledge. To incorporate new information, we've created a semantic-driven method that leverages the system's existing knowledge base and represents the integration challenge as a set of answer-specific instructions. These instructions guide the existing question answering model in identifying the domain of interest and assessing the type of unknown entity, thereby facilitating more effective knowledge acquisition. Empirical evidence from two distinct datasets supports the validity of this innovative method, which outperforms existing integration techniques and demonstrates significant difficulty for standard deep learning models to master independently. To facilitate further investigation, our group has made the instruction-based model, integration strategy, and training data readily accessible through Docker, which aids in efficiently replicating and expanding upon our work.

Applied tasks like image recognition require models to process vast amounts of data, which can be computationally intensive. Deep learning faces significant efficiency challenges due to limited resources, particularly when training models on data stored in multiple locations. To address these issues, researchers have developed techniques for distributed training, including methods for model partitioning, where the model is split into smaller parts, each trained on a separate device. However, this approach leads to considerable communication overhead, as the model's partitioned parts must be synchronized frequently. To mitigate this problem, scientists have explored using random walks, where data within its storage location is perturbed before being shared with other parts of the model. Although initial results were promising, the random walk approach requires precise step lengths, which are difficult to determine accurately. This difficulty is especially pronounced in scenarios with varying device speeds, leading to subopt性能 when devices have different capabilities, as observed in experimental evaluations.

A significant correlation exists between individuals involved in criminal activities and those suffering from untreated mental health issues. To investigate the impact of closing free mental health clinics on criminal activities, an analysis was conducted using historical data from Los Angeles County, which exhibited sudden closure of these facilities. Through this analysis, an estimated 14 new imprisonable crimes per closing were observed, with the most affected categories being violent activities, theft, and weapons-related offenses. The results also indicated that these activities did not migrate to other areas but instead remained concentrated in the original community. By plugging in local data, an estimated $1.1 million in additional victim compensation went unclaimed annually per clinic closure. This study's implications extend beyond Los Angeles, highlighting the necessity for robust public policy assessments that rely on exogenous variations in independent variables.

For IHSES, a new iterative semi-supervised learning framework is proposed in the context of noisy label learning for 3D medical image segmentation. This innovative method derives supervision information from just the most-segmented modality in multi-modal images, making it particularly effective when performance degrades due to using only single-modality data. Interpolation-based mixing is employed to generate and replace multi-modal segmentation results, yielding a iterative refinement approach that can achieve better results than dealing with single-modality segmentation. A key feature of IHSES is its lack of dependency on the number of modality inputs, enabling it to deliver consistent performance across various input configurations. Experimental evidence from multiple datasets in kidney and brain tumor segmentation demonstrates the effectiveness of IHSES, showing consistent improvement over methods of interpolation and handling single-modality data.

The structural properties of materials are closely linked to the local arrangements of atoms. In order to understand and predict the behavior of materials, it is crucial to quantify these atomic configurations in a way that is meaningful to both humans and machine learning models. Recently, graph neural networks have been widely used to analyze images of atoms, leveraging the power of deep learning to extract features and classify atomic structures. However, while these models demonstrate high performance, their ability to generalize to new data is limited, and more importantly, they lack interpretability. In this paper, we introduce the concept of Local Atomic Weights (LAW), a new method for representing atomic structures that are derived from continuous values. We show that LAW can be applied to a range of settings, including supervised learning tasks, reinforcement learning, and optimization. Through multiple case studies using state-of-the-art graph neural networks, we demonstrate the practical benefits of LAW in improving model performance and providing human and machine-interpretable insights into the training data, as well as the internal representations learned by the models. Moreover, we have made the LAW code publicly available to facilitate further research and development in the field of materials science.

Deep learning models for knowledge tracing have been applied to assess students' subject matter knowledge, but evaluating their effectiveness remains a significant challenge due to the substantial manual work involved in creating training data. This project leverages large-scale data from a popular online platform, Duokeen, to educate and test deep learning models, examining the feasibility of using real-world data on a massive scale. Our study employs data from over 100,000 students across 4,000 courses, analyzing student performance in various subject matter areas. With this extensive dataset, we investigate the effectiveness of state-of-the-art deep learning methods, revealing that recent models like DT and AT exhibit marginally better results than the traditional BAYES approach but also experience drops in performance when faced with new data. Our findings also reveal inconsistencies in the results of deep learning models, calling for reevaluation of their evaluation methods, and emphasize the significance of student and course attributes in predicting student performance, which current deep learning models fail to capture.

For an class of second-order elliptic operators with coefficients that vary spatially, we establish a relationship between them and a operator that is guaranteed to be surjective, specifically for a given condition, it is found that they are not generally invertible. As a consequence, we discover that for any given smooth function, solving the initial elliptic operator to match this function is not always feasible. To demonstrate this, we examine specific cases where the initial operator does not satisfy the condition required for its regularity, it is shown that there are given smooth functions that it cannot produce.

We have updated and tested the format with various existing tools, yielding successful outcomes in combining them and creating a combined solver for SMT problems.

We've developed a new private learning method called FedBuff that combines scaled gradient aggregation to increase efficiency and two-person authentication to maintain security. As we add more processing units, our scalability breakthrough lets us handle enormous datasets without compromising privacy. This becomes evident when we test with as little as one processing unit and see how performance improves with more units. The algorithm's end-to-end code is available on GitHub.

Recent advances in automatic speech recognition using transfer learning have mostly focused on improving efficiency by utilizing spoken language resources from more efficient backbones. While effective, this approach neglects the potential application of transfer learning beyond language efficiency. To assess whether speech transfer learning between two distinct languages yields beneficial outcomes, an experiment was conducted using the Montague Architecture on the Jaeger dataset, which includes spoken English and Jaeger languages. Although results from using a high-efficiency structure were promising, unexpected findings emerged when experimenting with the lighter architecture. Furthermore, large efficiency gains were achieved when starting with the spoken Jaeger language. To further understand these results, an experiment was carried out using the Montague Architecture on the Mozilla Common Voice dataset, which comprises ten different languages, demonstrating that speech transfer learning between languages with less similarity may actually harm speech recognition performance when using the same target efficiency. Furthermore, large efficiency gains when starting with the spoken Jaeger language were achieved. To validate these findings using the Mozilla Common Voice dataset, large efficiency gains when starting with the spoken Jaeger language were achieved.

Underwater environments pose unique challenges for mobile devices due to signal reflections and delays caused by constrained bandwidth. These issues make efficient data transmission difficult, leading to increased complexity in real-time decision-making. In this study, we focus on improving the accuracy of value estimation during data transfer difficulties for mobile devices navigating underwater settings. Specifically, we develop the SPGP-SARSA algorithm, which enhances the conventional GPR-SARSA method by incorporating a guided strategy for accuracy improvement. This novel approach leverages a Subset SARSA technique to refine value estimation and reduce data transmission delays. Furthermore, a Guided Policy network is employed to generate an accurate policy by filtering out irrelevant experiences and identifying the most pertinent ones to update the current value estimation. Through comprehensive experiments, our proposed method demonstrates enhanced performance compared to conventional SPGP-SARSA and GPR-SARSA approaches in terms of value estimation accuracy and overall task completion.

Although transfer learning techniques have achieved significant success in various natural language processing tasks, they face considerable challenges when applied to sequence-labeling tasks with a small amount of target domain data. This is particularly evident in error correction scenarios, where sequences often contain numerous annotation errors that hinder performance. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel error correction adaptation method that leverages source domain knowledge and is enhanced with pretraining, allowing it to correct multiple sequence annotation errors and improve performance on target tasks. Notably, our method does not require any lossless training data and has shown state-of-the-art results in several sequence-labeling tasks containing significant amounts of noisy labels. Furthermore, performance evaluations have established that our GEC adaptation approach outperforms traditional multi-task transfer learning methods, even with small amounts of clean target domain data. Extensive experiments were conducted to validate these findings.

In cooperative division of continuous and divisible goods among multiple agents, simple mechanisms like Round-Robin and Cut-and-Chose are commonly used to allocate portions. Our research focuses on the analysis of Round-Robin within this context, specifically an variant where multiple agents simultaneously select portions from remaining unallocated portions, in contrast to the traditional single-agent variant. Our study also extends to more complex scenarios involving multiple rounds of selection and instances with several distinct types of goods, all modeled using an N-dimensional matrix. Our analysis reveals that Round-Robin ensures an allocation that is weakly approximate envy-free, improving upon previous findings in (N-dimensional) settings. Additionally, our variant demonstrates that Round-Robin allocates portions in a way that is roughly self-fixing and weakly approximate envy-free, in contrast to Cut-and-Chose obtaining portions in a way is not necessarily self-fixing or envy-free fair. Our results are all guaranteed regardless of the number of people, parts, dimensions, randomization, and in our basic setting, regardless of individual preferences, in contrast to Cut-and-Chose, which requires specific assumptions about preferences to ensure self-fulfilling and approximate envy-free fairness. Furthermore, our analysis of Round-Robin is conducted in a basic deterministic setting, in contrast to Cut-and-Chose, which requires consideration of multiple instances, randomization, and so on to ensure self-fulfilling and approximate envy-free fairness.

We analyzed the optical spectra of the GTC instrument obtained for the UGC 8839 galaxy, focusing on its HII regions, to understand its star formation processes. Located at a 12.4 megaparsecs distance, this galaxy exhibits very active star formation in its outer regions. The UGC 8839's properties were compared to similar galaxies, SNG 694 and NGC 5253, to better understand its evolution. The galaxies' HII regions were categorized based on their distances from the galaxy's center, to identify the location of their main star formation areas. The galaxies' g-r maps and rotation curves were also studied to understand how mass is distributed within them. The UGC 8839's large bulge contributes significantly to its total mass within a certain radius, but beyond that, the galaxies' mass is dominated by their dark matter halos, which may influence their star formation processes, as seen in the UGC 8839's outer regions, where the halo's influence is most pronounced.

Using state-of-the-art QCD lattice data, we've examined the behavior of scalar, pseudoscalar, and tensor scalar quark currents in relation to meson masses. By analyzing a wide range of quark mass combinations that result in both charged and neutral mesons, we mapped the current-meson mass relations for pseudoscalar (U-spin), singlet, and tensor (D-spin) categories. Our findings show that the differences between charged and corresponding neutral meson masses provide insights into lattice QCD predictions. Notably, the lattice data indicates that the tensor current does not differentiate between charged and their corresponding neutral meson masses, suggesting that the $g_{T}$ coupling in the Standard Model effective field theory Lagrangian does not generate a mass difference in the second generation of quarks. Furthermore, our study reveals that the differences between charged and their corresponding neutral meson masses offer insights into the strong and electromagnetic components of the two-point function. As the lattice data's quark mass variations do not extend to heavier quarks, the integrals of these components can only be partially validated through QCD sum rules.

We analyzed the extensive variability in accretion rates of the classical T Tauri star DO Psc over a continuous 18-month observational period, revealing that extreme accretion rate fluctuations can significantly hinder our ability to draw conclusions about disk evolution based solely on stellar properties. Despite the overall mean behavior, we found that in some instances, accretion rate variability exhibited "excursions" of up to five orders of magnitude, with a standard deviation exceeding its mean by a factor of ten. We drew comparisons with similar studies of other T Tauri stars, such as GSC 06142 and GG Tauri A, and discussed how extreme variability challenges prevailing theories of disk evolution, which often fail to account for such substantial fluctuations. We also explored the concept that extreme variability may be a common characteristic of T Tauri disks, with long-term studies of disk variability being crucial for developing more accurate models of disk evolution and disk-planet interactions.

SIT, also known as Shared Individual Trajectories, is a novel framework for offline multi-agent settings. In this approach, the joint observations and actions of all agents in the offline dataset are reorganized into separate trajectories based on individual agent experiences. By training a model directly on these real SITs, each agent's learned policy is equivalent to that trained on aggregated values in traditional methods, but with a significant reduction in difficulty for offline data. Furthermore, with additional ease, offline and easy-to-master multi-agent problems can be solved by combining real and simulated SITs. Extensive experiments on hard multi-agent environments with deep reinforcement learning demonstrate the superiority of SIT over current state-of-the-art methods.

Recently, convolutional neural networks have shown great potential in processing high-dimensional data, including applications with convolutional architectures like U-Nets for medical image segmentation using limited samples. This work explores using a convolutional autoencoder to perform registration of two-dimensional images, combining the dimensionality reduction capabilities of autoencoders with the reception and sharing of features in convolutional architectures. We compare our proposed method to an intensity-based registration approach using gradient descent and find that combining autoencoders and convolutional architectures yields beneficial results. Furthermore, we compare various configurations of our proposed network and offer guidance on their respective performances.

Quantum mechanics raises intriguing questions about its implications for reality, particularly due to nonlocal effects and the capacity for steering, both of which depend on the location of a system's components. These effects also require interactions between parts, yet they are typically observed in single, isolated systems. This seems contradictory, particularly in the case of a single photon or an atom with a single excited electron, which can be both locally isolated and participate in nonlocal or steering scenarios simultaneously. We find this situation paradoxical and thus propose a framework for single-particle entanglement that extends beyond its current limited definitions, situated at the intersection of nonlocality and steering. We then demonstrate the sufficiency of this concept by showing how the "entangled" state of light's polarization can arise from either scenario, requiring only a single beam splitter for realization. This finding is further supported by the development of more complex, realistically verifiable predictions involving two beam splitters. Current experiments can already provide initial evidence of this phenomenon, paving the way for exploring more complex, nonlocal and steering-based cases.

To ensure data security, reliability, and privacy in Internet of Vehicles systems, multiple researchers have explored various applications of Blockchain technology. Despite the existence of multiple Blockchain-based IVOS security protocols, there is a lack of organized information on existing solutions and their comparative analysis. To address this issue, this study provides a comprehensive review of Blockchain technology and its potential applications in improving security within IVOS. Furthermore, this study evaluates existing Blockchain-based IVOS security protocols in terms of their ability to manage malicious behaviors, validate data integrity, and protect user privacy. Furthermore, this study explores possible future research directions in this area.

Ten epochs of observations were conducted using the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer for the binary system V392 Per over a 996-day period following its nova eruption. Initial observations indicated extensive hydrogen line emission and low ionized sulfur levels, suggesting an eruption with relatively low accreted material. As time passed, these characteristics started to diminish, giving V392 Per its typical post-eruption appearance. The system's behavior can be explained by a disk that was partially filled and underwent a phase of nova growth. Post-eruption, V392 Per continued to exhibit high-sensitivity to accretion conditions for at least two years, before transitioning to lower accretion conditions. Post-POSED stages were observed in ten occasions with FUSE, and the system's state remained similar across these instances. However, in a delayed instance 14 days before these instances, V392 Per entered a high-sensitivity state again, before transitioning back to lower accretion conditions. The system's disk appears to have been displaced to a phase with a high-sensitivity condition following its eruption, before eventually transitioning to lower accretion conditions.

The Lloyd-based pilot scheduling method exhibits optimal pilot overhead for user equipment employing maximum ratio transmission, yet its training overhead remains excessively high for massive MIMO systems with many antennas. Moreover, pilot overhead in the Lloyd method escalates rapidly due to the need for extensive training signals. In response, this study proposes a novel pilot encoding feedback scheme that minimizes pilot overhead and is well-suited for pilot encoding. In addition, this scheme delivers superior performance compared to Lloyd methods, achieving superior achievable rates with lower pilot overhead. The scheme's outstanding performance stems from its ability to determine optimal pilot lengths, shapes, and precoders without extensive training signals, in contrast, Lloyd methods require extensive training signals to determine optimal pilot lengths. The proposed scheme's efficiency and superior performance have been validated through extensive numerical results.

Currents that occur at surface boundaries and resist disruption in open systems with infinite lattices are investigated and calculated for the 2D Harper model. We examine the stability of these currents when the system goes from an idealized isolated state to a realistic finite-hypercubic lattice. The resistance to disruption varies significantly based on the shape of the lattice, with surface currents proving more persistent in lattices with greater asymmetry. The harmonic dressing of a surface current from a specific plane can be seen from its total momentum and results in backscattering between opposite momenta on the harmonic spectrum. The resistance to disruption of these currents increases with the size of the system and the strength of harmonic confinement, but also depends on the relationship between the discrete momentum and the direction of movement. The harmonic dressing also gives the harmonic harmonic Hall conductance at the surface, with a value half that of the infinite system's conductance in certain conditions.

In Brans-Dicke theory, we investigate whether a star that has been shaken will be able to release its energy as radiation made up of scalar gravitational waves to an infinite distance, or if it remains trapped within the star's surface. In this study, we find that if a star has an average density below a certain threshold determined by the Brans-Dicke parameter $\omega$, the energy it loses to the infinite distance is negligible; however, if the star's density exceeds this threshold, the Brans-Dicke theory predicts the star will emit the infinite distance a significant fraction of its mass, much like a classic black hole. In this paper, we also explore ways to constrain this theory using observations of PSR J0952-0653 and N47.5, both of which provide evidence in favor of Brans-Dicke theory and suggest that it can be observed.

We examine the characteristics of a potential alternative to standard cosmological nucleosynthesis theory, specifically Population III binary black hole remnant mergers. Using stellar evolution simulations, we determined the final properties of low mass Population III stars and matched them to Population III gas in a redshifted universe. Based on these matches, we calculated the resulting binary black hole remnant population in a high early universe. We then estimated the merger rate density in the universe for this alternative scenario. The rate density peaks at z = 6.5 and reaches a value of 4.5e-9 Mgh^-3 pc^-3 year^-1 before declining at earlier times due to the lack of gas in Lyman limit systems. The rate density is 7.7e5 times greater than predicted in standard cosmological nucleosynthesis theory. The population III binary black hole remnant merger rate density can be constrained by combining observational data from the universe with a prior on the fraction of Population III stars.

This study focuses on secure joint beamforming and power management in an advanced wireless network. In this network, an ambitious base station transmits a signal to an honest user while preventing an eavesdropper from intercepting the signal. Due to limited network resources, the base station's energy consumption impacts how data is transmitted at another base station that communicates with the eavesdropper. We formulate a game-theoretic model to analyze this interaction, where the base stations cooperate to maximize security while keeping each other's power consumption within bounds. Our model optimizes two key allocation strategies: coherent combining at the receiver and power distribution among different transmission links. To solve this problem, we develop an iterative algorithm based on linear programming that finds the best power allocation among the base stations. To make things more manageable, we break down the complex problem into two simpler subproblems: one for power allocation and another for coherent combining. Our approach ensures that the eavesdropper remains unaware of the base station's power limitations. Numerical results show that this approach effectively minimizes what the eavesdropper can learn while also meeting all performance requirements.

In recent years, natural language simulations like TextWorld have garnered significant attention from researchers. However, substantial breakthroughs in this area require extensive simulations, which were historically limited due to unavailable high-performance simulation platforms. We introduce TextWorldExpress, an open simulation environment that enhances the performance of simulation tasks by a factor of fifty, outperforming previous platforms. Notably, TextWorldExpress achieves the efficient execution of 1200 simultaneous simulations in just one day. We make our enhanced simulation platform accessible to the community, along with a high-performance set of 10000+ text games compiled with the Rosetta2 architecture for both Intel and Apple M1 processors, enabling the continued development of text games and ecosystem participants.

Hardware based tensor decomposed models have demonstrated superior processing capabilities compared to software CPU implementations, however their specialized designs limit their versatility to specific types of workloads. We have developed a universal intelligence processing system called FDHT-LSTM, which utilizes compressed data representations through HOSR decomposition and LSTM algorithms, and can execute both specific LSTM hardware tasks and diverse non-hardware tasks. In our research, we have developed a dynamic control unit to manage FDHT-LSTM's processing unit, storage unit, and data compression unit to optimize its performance for various types of workloads. Our experimental results indicate that FDHT-FAPR-LSTM, which combines data compression and hardware based LSTM algorithms, outperforms FDHT-LSTM, traditional HOSR based systems, and shows a significant improvement in energy efficiency when processing mixed workloads consisting of data types. In comparison to FDHT-LSTM, our system shows enhanced energy efficiency and demonstrates that FDHT-FAPR-LSTM is most energy efficient when processing data that requires increased processing steps. In contrast, FDHT-LSTM, the system without data compression, shows improved throughput and energy efficiency when processing data that requires increased processing steps, including data cleaning, missing data estimation, and LSTM algorithms.
